title: Fabrication and Characterization of a Conformal Skin-like Electronic System for Quantitative, Cutaneous Wound Management
protocol: Cut a bare 3 in silicon (Si) wafer into the desired size for the wound device using a diamond blade.
Degrease Si wafer with acetone and isopropyl alcohol (IPA).
Rinse the wafer with deionized (DI) water and then dry with nitrogen.
Dehydrate the wafer on a hotplate at 110 °C for 3 min.
Prepare 11 g of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) mixture with a 10:1 volume ratio of base and curing agent.
Degas the PDMS mixture in a vacuum chamber for an hour.
Spin coat 5 g of mixed PDMS solution on the wafer at 3,000 rpm for 1 min.
Fully cure the coated wafer on a hotplate at 150 °C for 30 min.
Treat the PDMS-coated wafer with ultraviolet (UV)/ozone using a UV lamp (8.9 mW/cm²) for 3 min.
Spin coat polyimide (PI; 2 ml) on the PDMS coated wafer at 4,000 rpm for 1 min to form a 1.2-µm-thick layer.
Pre-bake the spin-coated PI layer on a hotplate at 150 °C for 5 min.
Post-bake the pre-baked layer at 250 °C for 2 hr.
Deposit chromium (Cr) to form a 20 nm-thick layer by using electron-beam evaporation.
Deposit copper (Cu) to form a 3 µm-thick layer by using electron-beam evaporation.
Monitor the film thickness during deposition by the deposition controller interface embedded in the evaporator.
Spin coat a photoresist (2 ml) with three steps: at 900 rpm for 10 sec, 1,100 rpm for 60 sec, and 4,000 rpm for 20 sec.
Cure the spin-coated photoresist on a hotplate at 75 °C for 30 min.
Align Cu electronic patterns on the Si wafer using a UV aligner (power: 10 mW/sec) for an exposure time of 25 seconds.
Develop the photoresist in a diluted base developer (1:2 ratio of developer and DI water) for one minute, then rinse with DI water and dry with nitrogen.
Inspect the patterns (Cu fractals and interconnects) using a microscope to confirm feature size and identify any defects from particulates.
Remove photoresist by rinsing with acetone/IPA/DI water if unwanted defects are present.
Repeat steps from 1.2.4 to 1.2.6 after drying the wafer with nitrogen if necessary.

Etch the Cu layer on the Si wafer by immersing in a wet chemical etchant (mixture of ammonium persulfate and water in ratio of 1:4) for approximately 6 minutes at 40 °C, then rinse with DI water and dry with nitrogen.
Inspect the patterns using a microscope to check for any over-etched areas.
Etch the Cr layer with reactive ion etching at a pressure of 300 mTorr, power of 200 W, CF4 gas flow rate of 5 sccm, and O2 gas flow rate of 10 sccm for 5 min.
Inspect the patterns after etching.
Remove remaining photoresist from metal layers by immersing the wafer in acetone (10 ml), IPA (10 ml), and DI water (20 ml).
Dry the wafer with nitrogen.
Spincoat PI (2 ml) on the metal deposited wafer at 4000 rpm for 1 min to form a 1.2-µm-thick layer.
Pre-bake the coated wafer on a hotplate at 150 °C for 5 min.
Post-bake the coated wafer at 250 °C for 2 hr.
Spincoat photoresist (2 ml) with three steps: 900 rpm for 10 sec, 1100 rpm for 60 sec, and 4000 rpm for 20 sec.
Cure the coated wafer on a hotplate at 75 °C for 30 min.
Align PI patterns to encapsulate Cu electronics with pre-defined Cu fractals and interconnects using a UV aligner (power: 10 mW/sec) with exposure time of 25 sec.
Develop the photoresist with a diluted developer (1:2 ratio) for one minute.
Rinse with DI water.
Dry with nitrogen.
Inspect patterns using a microscope to confirm feature size and defects.
Remove unwanted defects by rinsing with acetone/IPA/DI water.
Dry with nitrogen.
Repeat steps from 1.2.10 to 1.2.13 if necessary.
Etch the PI layer with RIE (pressure: 170 mTorr, power: 150 W, O2 gas: 20 sccm) for 25 minutes.
Inspect patterns after etching.
Remove remaining photoresist by immersing in acetone (10 ml), IPA (10 ml), and DI water (20 ml).
Dry with nitrogen.
Prepare a 10 g mixture of encapsulating silicone (1:1 volume ratio of base and curing agent) and add black ink in a one-to-one volume ratio.
Spincoat 8 g of the mixture at 150 rpm for 1 minute to form a 500 µm thick elastomeric membrane.
Cure the membrane at room temperature overnight.
Cut the membrane into a size of 70 mm x 30 mm using a sharp razor blade.
Gently detach the membrane from the petri dish.
Retrieve and transfer electronics.
Cut a water soluble tape (25 mm x 80 mm) and gently laminate onto the fabricated electronic patterns.
Place the laminated patterns on a hotplate at 130 °C for 3 min.
Detach the tape rapidly from the PDMS/Si wafer to retrieve the electronic patterns.
Deposit a 20 nm thick Cr followed by a 50 nm thick silicon dioxide (SiO2) on retrieved patterns by e-beam evaporation.
Treat UV/ozone using a UV lamp (365 nm, 8.9 mW/cm²) on the targeted silicone membrane for 2 min to activate the surface.
Transfer the patterns to the silicone membrane by placing them onto the tape and applying pressure from top side of the patterns down to the substrate.
Apply water to dissolve the tape for 5 min.
Peel off the tape, rinse with DI water, and dry on a hotplate at 90 °C for 1 min.
Prepare an encapsulating silicone mixture (1:1 volume ratio of base and curing agent).
Encapsulate the device using a silicone membrane.
Cover the cable contact pads with a rectangular PDMS piece by van der Waals bonding.
Spincoat the silicone mixture at 4,000 rpm for 1 min to form a 5 μm thick layer on the transferred electronics.
Cure the coated electronics at room temperature overnight.
Apply liquid steel flux (0.5 ml) on the connector pads using a pipette.
Bond a thin, flexible ribbon cable on the contact points with pressure at high temperature (>60 °C).
Check the electrical connection between the sensor pad and the film cable end using a digital multimeter.
Bond the other end of the ribbon cable to a customized printed circuit board using the same strategy.
Connect conventional wires to the PCB for connecting the device to data acquisition hardware.
Clean the device using a diluted disinfectant solution prepared in a 40:1 volume ratio of water and disinfectant.
Spray the solution (10 g) on the device.
Soak the device for 10 min.
Rinse with water three times.
Dry the device with clean tissues.
Prepare a lock-in amplifier.
Connect the lock-in amplifier to a current source.
Connect the lock-in amplifier to a multiplexer.
Install custom software on a laptop computer for data recording.
Place an infrared camera on a tripod and focus it on a target object for thermography as a reference.
Set system parameters of the lock-in amplifier to measure thermal conductivity (frequency: 1 & 3 Hz; time constant: 3 and 1 sec; sensitivity: 1 mV; dynamic reserve: high reserve).

Set system parameters of the lock-in amplifier to measure temperature (frequency: 997 Hz; time constant: 300 msec; sensitivity: 2 mV; dynamic reserve: low noise) with an applied constant current (2 mA).
Connect two wound devices, prepared by microfabrication and transfer printing, to the multiplexer.
Mount one wound device on a wound site and another on a contralateral site.
Record temperature data from the patient using the lock-in amplifier system.
Record thermal conductivity data from the patient using the lock-in amplifier system.
Gently rub the device application sites on the skin using antiseptic alcohol wipes.
Laminate two devices on desired skin locations by gently pressing the device to the skin with fingers.
Measure the electrical voltage (3Ω) of the device related to thermal conductivity.
Evaluate obtained data to verify conformal contact of the device to the skin; abnormal value (< 0.1 W/mK) shows bad contact.
Measure the electrical resistance to determine temperature distribution and record data through custom software.
Take optical images of two devices on the skin.
Take IR images of two devices on the skin.
Compare temperature values from the IR images with the data recorded from the wound device.
Add both sets of values to separate columns in a customized spreadsheet.
Export the recorded data to the customized template.
Automatically calculate temperature and thermal conductivity from an array of sensors in the device.
Plot the data (temperature and thermal conductivity according to sensor location) on different time scales for comparison over one month.
Analyze the data by comparing series of temperature and thermal conductivity values according to time.
Identify sudden elevations or drops indicating changes in wound healing phase or unexpected abnormalities.
